title: Assignment Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of assignment operators in C#.
Identify the relevant operand types, evaluation rules and result types.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: Assignment stores a value in a variable. The simple assignment operator (=) assigns the right-hand value to the left-hand variable. Compound assignment operators such as +=, -=, *=, /= and %= combine an operation with assignment. Bitwise compound assignments include &=, |=, ^=, <<= and >>=. The right-hand side is evaluated before the assignment takes effect; compound assignments also perform the operator's conversion rules, so they are not always identical in typing to writing the expanded expression.
understand.whyItMatters: Compound assignments keep counters, totals and state updates concise while preserving the intent of the operation.
understand.analogy: A compound assignment is like updating a running account balance with one clearly labelled adjustment.
understand.analogyLimit: Compound assignment can include an implicit conversion that the expanded expression would require you to write explicitly. Avoid dense chained assignments when they reduce readability.

explain.narrative:
## Simple assignment

The `=` operator assigns the value of an expression to a variable. It is not an equality comparison; comparison uses `==`.

## Compound assignment

Operators such as `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `%=` update an existing variable. For example, `score += 5` adds five and stores the result back in `score`. Bitwise compound assignments include `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=` and `>>=`.

## Evaluation and type behavior

The right-hand expression is evaluated before the assignment. Compound assignment is specified with conversion behavior that can differ from manually expanding the expression, especially with narrower numeric types. Use explicit casts when they improve clarity, and prefer simple statements over clever chains.

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.

questions.prompt: Why should a developer understand operand types?
